edge_rate_limit.was: Caddy forwarded X-Real-IP from CF-Connecting-IP unconditionally, on the assumption that Cloudflare sits in front. It does not 闂?the response headers show only Caddy 闂?so the header was empty, the API fell back to the socket peer, and every visitor on earth shared ONE bucket: 120 requests and 20 writes per minute for the entire deployment. Redis showed the proof: pg:rate:general:172.26.0.3 for traffic from unrelated networks.
edge_rate_limit.now: Caddy decides with a map: CF-Connecting-IP when present, {client_ip} otherwise. X-Real-IP stays the only address the API trusts (X-Forwarded-For is client-controllable and ignored). Applied by copying the Caddyfile to its bind-mount source and `caddy reload`; no image rebuild is involved.
edge_rate_limit.verified: buckets after the reload carry distinct visitor addresses (pg:rate:general:1.83.244.95, :34.87.50.183, ...) instead of the Caddy container's.

image_context_budget.was: a turn's images were unbounded. Measured on real inputs: a 2048px dense screenshot is ~600 KB of JPEG, which base64 turns into ~830 KB and the provider bills as roughly 200k input tokens, so a handful of phone screenshots in one turn could ask for a request the model's window cannot hold 鈥?and it would fail at the provider with no explanation.
image_context_budget.now: a turn stops collecting image bytes at AGENT_IMAGE_CONTEXT_BYTES (3 MB default), logs which images it left out, and still sends all attachment text. Fewer pictures beats a request the model cannot accept.

context_window.was: a freed attachment was replayed to the model from the message that stored it 闂?with its text gone, the model saw an empty document it could not tell apart from a real one, and a turn stored before the removal replayed text the user had just deleted. Separately, images could be re-sent on a later turn: the rule was one-way, so a newer text-only turn fell back to an older turn's pixels.
context_window.now: stored attachments are filtered by what still exists (removed ones go, and so do ids that are gone), and exactly one turn in the window 闂?the newest that attaches an image 闂?carries pixels.
context_window.verified: 16 tests in tests/unit/test_chat_workspace.py, including the removed-attachment replay and the single-image-turn rule across all three windows.

why.found_by: scripts/probe_chat_workspace.py, a probe that drives the real endpoints through a session and prints what happens
why.defect: the 100 MB attachment allowance was a one-way door. Quota is measured in stored bytes and NOTHING released them: DELETE /api/agent/attachments/{id} did not exist (404), no screen listed a user's uploads, and a user who reached the ceiling received 400 ATTACHMENT_STORAGE_LIMIT on every later upload with nothing to act on. Deleting a conversation did not release the bytes its attachments held either.
why.second_defect: a draft the user abandoned (uploaded, never sent) stayed stored forever while being invisible, and the composer's remove button only dropped it from local state, leaving the bytes behind.

what_changed: DELETE /api/agent/attachments/{id} frees one of the caller's own attachments. The row survives (name, mime, kind, sha256 are what a historical message renders) while payload and extracted text are dropped, and metadata now reports removed:true with an empty url so the UI can say what happened instead of linking to a 404. Downloading a freed file answers 410 ATTACHMENT_REMOVED, not 409.
Deleting a conversation releases the bytes its own messages had sent, and returns attachments_released. History rows are untouched: only the byte count is freed.
An upload older than 24 h that no message references is reclaimed when the allowance is next exhausted, so a full account recovers without the user having to find something to delete.
The send path skips an attachment it cannot resolve instead of failing the turn: a draft whose file was deleted before sending must not become an error.

The composer's remove button now calls the API and keeps the card as 閻庤鐡曠亸娆庣昂闂?Removed; the send button ignores removed files; a full allowance reports storage rather than advising the user to check the file format; an oversize file names the limit it hit.
The build script's mirror guard compared a fixed 8-character slice, so a 7-character short SHA was rejected; it now compares over the length the caller supplied.
The rollback script hard-coded one build directory and now derives the compose context from the pin file name, falling back to the newest complete build directory.
The release-verification script cleans up agent_attachments for its disposable account, which the first run left behind.

scheduler.state: running; holds pg:lock:scheduler with a renewed TTL
scheduler.note: this release fixed the underlying defect. The lock could name a container that no longer existed, so a crashed scheduler could never restart and every deploy had to wait out the holder TTL - sometimes twice, because the crash itself left the lock behind. reclaim_own_lock now clears a lock whose holder shares this container's hostname (a sibling instance always has its own container and therefore its own hostname), and a build_scheduler failure releases the lock instead of orphaning it. Verified live: the lock is held by this container's own hostname:pid and the TTL was renewed to ~900s while the process kept running, RestartCount 0.

follow_ups_not_shipped: the API rate limiter keys on the peer address it sees, which in production is the Caddy container rather than the visitor, so API_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=120 and EXPENSIVE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE=20 are effectively per-deployment budgets. Writes (uploads, agent runs) therefore share a 20/min ceiling across all users. Pre-existing; surfaced because acceptance runs make bursts of uploads and correctly receive 429. Needs a trusted client address forwarded from Caddy.
